TrendMart Retail, Inc. - Q3 FY2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the TrendMart Retail, Inc. Q3 FY2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, the instructions are to press star one on your telephone keypad if you would like to join the queue. Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss TrendMart Retail's results for the Q3 FY2024. Joining me on today’s call are Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer; David Patel, Chief Merchandising Officer; Emily Rodriguez, Chief Stores Officer; Alex Kim, Chief Marketing Officer; and Raj Singh, Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Mike Thompson.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report TrendMart Retail's performance for the Q3 FY2024. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Our brick-and-mortar network remains a powerhouse, generating meaningful sales productivity gains even as we navigate inflation pressures and shifting consumer behaviors. We saw strength across key categories like apparel, home goods, and beauty, with our stores serving as experiential hubs that complement our growing omnichannel presence. We're making progress on fleet optimization, supply chain resilience, and customer loyalty, all while keeping a tight lid on costs.

Today, we'll cover our progress in sales per square foot, regional performance variations, store remodel plans, shrink impacts, inventory turnover, inventory levels year-over-year, marketing expense trends, and key strategic initiatives. We're confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa Chen to provide more details on our financial results.

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Mike. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the Q3 FY2024.

Our total revenue for the quarter was $2.3 billion, a 4.8% increase compared to the same period last year, driven by comparable store sales growth of 3.2% and contributions from new store openings. Breaking this down further, a cornerstone productivity measure for our brick-and-mortar footprint is sales per square foot, or SPSF, which we calculate as net sales divided by average selling square footage, excluding non-revenue areas like stockrooms and offices. This metric ties directly into rent leverage, inventory efficiency, and return on invested capital, especially with real estate costs averaging 8-12% of sales in our industry.

Q3 SPSF came in at $478 per square foot, up 4.2% year-over-year from $459 in Q3 FY2023. On a two-year basis, that's a 12.8% improvement from the $424 seen in Q3 FY2022 amid pandemic disruptions. Across our 1,450 stores averaging 25,000 selling square feet per location, this drove our headline sales figure. Full-year FY2024 SPSF is tracking at $465, on pace for the midpoint of our $462 to $468 guidance—our strongest since FY2019's pre-COVID $472 peak.

By category, apparel and accessories led at $512 per square foot, up 6.1% year-over-year, thanks to refined assortments in denim and activewear, including our private-label Urban Edge line that delivered 15% comparable uplift. Home goods was at $421, up 2.8%, as consumers shifted away from big-ticket items under 3.2% core inflation. Beauty and fragrance excelled at $689, powered by experiential setups like fragrance bars that increased dwell time 18%.

This marks six straight quarters of positive SPSF inflection, countering prior declines from e-commerce pressures. Traffic conversion rose 120 basis points to 28.5%, average unit retail climbed 2.7% to $48.50, and units per transaction stayed at 2.4. Smaller Express stores under 15,000 square feet hit $612, 28% above flagships, validating our pivot to denser urban formats similar to strategies at Macy's and Nordstrom Rack.

Regionally, there was notable dispersion, which played into our overall 3.2% comps. Sunbelt areas like Florida, Texas, and Arizona achieved $505 per square foot, up 7.1% year-over-year, with 5.2% same-store sales growth from migration and tourism—our Miami-Dade stores added 2.2 inventory turns. Northeast stores were at $442, flat year-over-year, hit by warm weather hurting outerwear and T.J. Maxx competition. Midwest held at $468, supported by value promotions lifting average ticket 4.1%. Our 120 Canadian stores reached $492 CAD, or about $360 USD, up 3.9% despite forex drag.

Key drivers include our SpaceMax remodels, complete in 420 stores or 32% of the chain, which shifted 12% of space to high-velocity areas like Levi's and Dyson shop-in-shops, delivering $620 incremental SPSF with under 18-month payback. AI planogramming with SymphonyAI boosted assortment velocity 22% via local tweaks, such as surfwear in California. Omnichannel like BOPIS and ship-from-store, now 18% of sales, added $25 per square foot effectively. Experiential TrendHub zones with AR mirrors and cafes in 150 stores lifted traffic 14% and $75 incremental SPSF. Loyalty members generated 2.3 times the SPSF of non-members.

We closed 45 low performers averaging $320 SPSF, freeing $120 million for 25 new Express stores aiming for $600-plus. Q4 SPSF guides to $495-$505, or 5-7% growth, with FY2025 at $485 overall and $700 for Express formats, aided by RFID for 10% accuracy gains and 1.2% shrinkage.

Gross margin was 34.8%, down 130 basis points year-over-year from 36.1%, influenced by several factors. Excluding mix benefits from private-label kitchen growth and 20 basis points from vendor markdowns, pressures came from promotions at 60 basis points, tariffs on textiles at 40 basis points, and shrink at 30 basis points. Shrink hit 1.9% of net sales, up from 1.6%, or $28 million lost, with external theft at 45% or 85 basis points.

Shrink breakdown: theft/external 0.85% (45%, up 25% year-over-year on electronics accessories, beauty tools, apparel); internal 0.25% (13%, stable); damage/admin 0.8% (42%). This has risen 20% since FY2021 with traffic rebound, worse in self-checkout stores (40% of mix, up 18%). Urban high-risk markets like California and New York (35% of base) saw 2.4%, up 30% from policy changes; suburban at 1.6%; rural 1.2%.

We're investing $45 million in loss prevention, up 25%, targeting 15-20% reduction by FY2025. AI cameras from Eagle Eye in 60% of stores detect 92% accurately, down incidents 22%; RFID/EAS with Levi's and P&G on 15 million units cuts walk-offs 30%; self-checkout with facial/weight tech deters 14%; BOPIS at 70% reduces handling; ORC task force recovered $2.1 million. Q4 shrink to 1.7%, aiding margin recovery.

Operating expenses were $1.19 billion, representing 51.7% of revenue, with marketing and advertising at $152 million, up 12% or 3.6% of sales—above our 3.0-3.5% target. Traditional media fell to 22% or $33 million, with CPMs up 15% to $25 and ROAS at 2.8x. Digital surged to 68% or $104 million, led by performance at 45%: Google Shopping CPC steady at $1.85, ROAS 5.2x; TikTok/Instagram up 35% to $18 million, lifting traffic 14% via shoppable AR. In-store at 10% or $15 million boosted baskets 22% with beacons. CAC down 9% to $22, LTV $312.

U.S. up 14% with hyper-local SEM; Europe 8% under GDPR; Asia-Pacific 25% on WeChat. Storefront 360 with Salesforce/Adobe cuts waste 11%, guiding to 3.4% in Q4 with $20 million holiday push for 6x ROAS.

Net income was $152 million, or $1.25 per share. We generated $285 million in cash flow from operations. Inventory levels ended at $1.28 billion, down 14% year-over-year—fourth straight quarter of declines, to lowest since Q1 2020. Inventory-to-sales at 11.2 weeks from 13.4, turns at 9.2x trailing twelve months from 7.9x. SKU cuts of 18% focused on high-velocity private labels at 62%; AI WMS/RFID reduced errors 22%, stockouts to 3.2%; VMI at 35%, pipeline down 30% to $185 million. Sunbelt down 18%, Northeast/Midwest 10%. Markdowns to 8.5% from 12.2%, adding 110 basis points to margins. Q4 down another 8-10%.

Full-year inventory turnover was 3.9x, up from 3.4x, strongest since FY2019's 4.1x; Q3 at 4.2x versus peers like Kohl's 3.8x. Average inventory down 12% to $2.8 billion despite 4% COGS growth to $10.9 billion; DIO to 94 from 107 days. Northeast/Midwest 4.2x on apparel; Southeast 3.5x from weather; West 4.0x. AI with Blue Yonder covers 85% SKUs, cuts stockouts/overstocks; RFID in 70% stores; BOPIS 18%. FY2024 target 4.2-4.4x via private label at 5.5x, micro-DCs, dynamic planning, vendor scorecards.

On remodels, our NextGen Store Refresh commits $275 million over FY24-26 for 180 stores or 22% of 820 core units—wait, scaling to our 1,450 fleet, it's 12% coverage prioritized. Per-store $1.4 million average, funded 60% free cash flow. Pilots in 25 stores showed +11.2% comps, traffic +18%, dwell +22%, ticket +6%, BOPIS efficiency +25%. Features: dynamic digital with RFID shelves/beacons for 3-5% upsell; LEED Silver with 20-25% utility cuts; experiential pods like home cafes/AR mirrors. Sunbelt 45% rollout for +14% comps; Midwest lite remodels; Northeast/West flagships with micro-DC. Projected 22-28% IRR, $450 million EBITDA add by FY26; small-format conversions next.

Key initiatives update: comps +3.2% beat industry 2.1%; margins +110 bps. Fleet: closed 45 Midwest stores, saving $18 million; opened 18 small-format Sunbelt with +15.2% comps; 25 more FY24. Omnichannel: BOPIS 28%, app downloads +27%, digital 32% sales. Supply chain: Reno DC cuts times 18 days; turns 5.3x, private label +250 bps. Loyalty: 62 million members at 62% sales. Experience zones lift ticket 16%.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Now, I'd like to hand it over to David Patel, our Chief Merchandising Officer, to discuss our new product lines, followed by Emily Rodriguez to discuss store operations, Alex Kim to discuss marketing initiatives, and Raj Singh to talk about technology advancements.

David Patel, Chief Merchandising Officer:
Thank you, Lisa. This quarter, we launched our expanded Urban Edge apparel and UrbanLiving Essentials home lines, which have seen strong uptake with 15% comps in denim/activewear and gains in kitchen textiles. Private labels now at 42% penetration, turning faster with higher margins. We're excited about upcoming beauty expansions and localized assortments, leveraging AI planogramming for 22% velocity gains.

Emily Rodriguez, Chief Stores Officer:
Thank you, David. We continue to focus on improving the customer experience in our stores. We have implemented SpaceMax remodels and NextGen refreshes in over 420 locations, reallocating space for high-velocity zones and experiential areas, yielding $620 incremental SPSF and 18% traffic lifts. Express formats and closures of underperformers are enhancing productivity, with new Sunbelt doors ramping quickly.

Alex Kim, Chief Marketing Officer:
Thank you, Emily. Our omnichannel campaigns, including TikTok shoppables and Google Shopping, have driven 14% traffic uplift and 5.2x ROAS. Loyalty Rewards engagement hit 62% of sales, with personalized bundles boosting conversion. Holiday activations will target 6x ROAS.

Raj Singh, Chief Technology Officer:
Thank you, Alex. We have invested in AI demand sensing with Blue Yonder and SymphonyAI, RFID across 70-85% of stores, and computer vision for loss prevention, improving turns, accuracy, and reducing shrink 22%. Edge computing and RetailOS enable real-time planograms and BOPIS at 28%.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. The floor is now open for questions. Our first question comes from John Ramirez with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Ramirez (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of regional performance variations on your sales, especially Sunbelt versus Northeast?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thanks, John. Regionally, we saw clear dispersion: Northeast comps down 0.9% from winter weather and urban housing softness, with traffic -2.1%, though remodels lifted BOPIS 15%. Midwest +1.5% on housing resilience and private labels. South shone at +6.2% with migration, housing starts +7.1%, traffic +4.3%. West +3.7%, strong in Mountain areas but softer California. This nets our 3.2% overall, with investments tilted South/West.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Maria Lopez with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Maria Lopez (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Good question, Maria. Q4 comps guide to 3-5%, building on holiday densification, 20% more gifting capacity, and easing inflation. Sunbelt momentum, remodel paybacks, and omnichannel at 28% BOPIS support this, with SPSF 5-7% up.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Kim with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Kim (Morgan Stanley):
Can you elaborate on the supply chain improvements and inventory discipline?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Absolutely, David. Reno DC cut Asia transit 18 days, freight 12%; VMI 35%, nearshoring lead times to 32 days; micro-fulfillment pilots shave DIO. Turns to 5.3x, inventory down 14% YoY with AI forecasting errors at 5%, RFID reducing shrinkage.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Sarah Patel with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Sarah Patel (Bank of America):
What is the impact from shrink and theft, and your mitigation plans?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Shrink pressured margins 30 bps at 1.9%, theft 0.85% up 25% in urban stores. But $45 million CapEx in AI cameras (92% detection), RFID/EAS, self-checkout tech, BOPIS, and ORC efforts reduced incidents 22%, recoveries $2.1 million. Q4 to 1.7%.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Chris Wong with Citigroup. Please go ahead.

Chris Wong (Citigroup):
Thoughts on marketing spend trends and remodel ROI?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Marketing up 12% to 3.6% of sales, digital 68% with 5.2x ROAS, CAC down 9%. Guides to 3.4% Q4. Remodels: $275 million for 180 stores, pilots +11.2% comps, 22-28% IRR, payback 24 months, $450 million EBITDA by FY26.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
